tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Five claims about word pairs that careful writers still swap in academic and public-affairs prose. Decide whether each account of meaning or spelling is accurate.
statements: In "The committee was not adverse to reopening the inquiry", the adjective is correctly chosen, since "adverse" describes a person's reluctance.
"Continuous" is the right choice for repeated interruptions separated by gaps, as in "The seminar was broken up by continuous questions from the back row".
"Immanent" is the spelling for something about to happen, so a seismologist warning of a likely aftershock would report that one is "immanent".
"Discrete" means separate and individually distinct, so a statistician who counts "discrete" categories of rainfall has chosen the correct spelling.
A driver who openly ignores a speed limit is said to "flaunt" the law, since "flaunt" means to break a rule with contempt.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In "The committee was not adverse to reopening the inquiry", the adjective is correctly chosen, since "adverse" describes a person's reluctance.**

"Averse" is the adjective for a person's disinclination and it collocates with to, as in averse to reopening a case. "Adverse" describes unfavourable circumstances or effects, such as adverse weather, an adverse ruling or an adverse drug reaction. What the committee lacks here is unwillingness rather than hostile conditions, so the slot belongs to the disinclination word.

**Tip:** If "reluctant" fits the frame, the word you want is averse.

The sentence reports an attitude, not a circumstance, so the defence of "adverse" collapses — "The committee was not averse to reopening the inquiry".

**B) "Continuous" is the right choice for repeated interruptions separated by gaps, as in "The seminar was broken up by continuous questions from the back row".**

"Continuous" describes something unbroken in space or time, like a continuous line of pylons or the continuous hum of a ventilation system. "Continual" describes something that keeps recurring with pauses between the episodes, which is exactly what a series of separate questions amounts to. Each interruption stops before the next begins, so the recurring-event adjective is the one this frame needs.

The gaps between the questions rule out the unbroken reading, so the recommendation misfires — "The seminar was broken up by continual questions from the back row".

**C) "Immanent" is the spelling for something about to happen, so a seismologist warning of a likely aftershock would report that one is "immanent".**

"Imminent" means about to occur at any moment, which is how forecasters and seismologists describe a hazard already at the door. "Immanent" is a philosophical and theological word meaning inherent or indwelling, as in a force immanent in nature, and it carries no reference to timing at all. A warning about an aftershock is a claim about the very near future.

**Trap:** The doubled m looks learned, but only the i-spelling means close in time.

Nearness is precisely what the seismologist is asserting, so the spelling recommended here is the wrong twin — the warning is that an aftershock is "imminent".

**D) "Discrete" means separate and individually distinct, so a statistician who counts "discrete" categories of rainfall has chosen the correct spelling.**

"Discrete" means separate, individually countable and non-overlapping, which is why data that fall into distinct bins are called discrete rather than continuous. "Discreet" is the social adjective for tact and careful silence, as in a discreet enquiry or a discreet word afterwards. Rainfall bands are exactly the separate, countable classes the first spelling names.

**Tip:** The two e's stand apart in "discrete", just like the categories it labels.

The statistical sense and the spelling on the page line up, so the description is sound.

**E) A driver who openly ignores a speed limit is said to "flaunt" the law, since "flaunt" means to break a rule with contempt.**

"Flout" means to defy a rule or convention openly, which is why drivers flout speed limits and developers flout planning conditions. "Flaunt" means to display something ostentatiously and takes the thing shown off as its object, as in flaunting wealth or flaunting a new title. The driver here is defying a regulation, not parading one, so the defiance verb is required.

Rules are flouted rather than flaunted, so the claim has the pair the wrong way round: the driver "flouts" the law.
tasks.solution_overview: Each line here turns on a single letter or a single sense, so read for the situation before you read for the spelling: circumstances or attitude for adverse and averse, unbroken or recurring for continuous and continual, nearness in time or inherence for imminent and immanent. Where two forms sound identical, ask which part of speech and which collocation the sentence has already committed to, as with discrete categories and a discreet enquiry. Slotting the other member of the pair into the frame is the quickest way to hear which one the sentence actually wants.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Each line below describes how a pair of similar-looking words behaves in academic, legal or medical writing. Decide whether the description matches standard usage.
statements: "Historical" is reserved for events judged important enough to shape what follows, so the first Moon landing is best called a "historical" moment.
"Credulous" describes an account that deserves to be believed, as in "The witness gave a credulous account of the fire".
Attendance that a university requires of every first-year student is "compulsive" attendance, because "compulsive" is the adjective for an obligation imposed from outside.
"Prone" means lying face down and "supine" means lying on the back, so a physiotherapist who asks a patient to move from "supine" to "prone" is asking for a roll onto the stomach.
"Apathy" is an absence of feeling or interest while "antipathy" is active dislike, so voters who cannot be bothered to turn out display "apathy" rather than antipathy.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Historical" is reserved for events judged important enough to shape what follows, so the first Moon landing is best called a "historical" moment.**

"Historic" marks an event as momentous, one that will be remembered and that alters the course of what comes after. "Historical" simply means belonging to history or dealing with the past, as in historical records, historical linguistics or a historical novel. A first landing on another world is being praised for its significance, which is the job of the shorter adjective.

**Tip:** Every event is historical once it is over; only a few are historic.

Significance rather than mere pastness is the point being made, so the label offered here is the weaker of the two: the landing was a "historic" moment.

**B) "Credulous" describes an account that deserves to be believed, as in "The witness gave a credulous account of the fire".**

"Credible" describes something worth believing, so evidence, testimony and threats can all be credible. "Credulous" describes a person who believes too readily, which is why we speak of a credulous audience or a credulous investor rather than a credulous statement. An account under scrutiny in court is being judged for its believability, not accused of gullibility.

**Trap:** Both words descend from credere, to believe, but one looks at the claim and the other at the listener.

The sentence weighs the testimony rather than the witness's naivety, so the label does not fit — "The witness gave a credible account of the fire".

**C) Attendance that a university requires of every first-year student is "compulsive" attendance, because "compulsive" is the adjective for an obligation imposed from outside.**

"Compulsory" describes something required by a rule or authority, as in compulsory military service, compulsory purchase or a compulsory module. "Compulsive" describes behaviour driven by an inner urge that is hard to resist, as in compulsive checking or a compulsive gambler. A university regulation is an external requirement, so the rule-based adjective is the one the sentence needs.

An institutional demand is not an inner urge, so the description fails: the seminars are "compulsory" for first-year students.

**D) "Prone" means lying face down and "supine" means lying on the back, so a physiotherapist who asks a patient to move from "supine" to "prone" is asking for a roll onto the stomach.**

"Prone" places the body face down, which is why clinicians speak of proning a patient to improve oxygenation. "Supine" places the body on its back, and it has a figurative sense of passive acquiescence as well, as in a supine parliament. Moving from the back to the face-down position is precisely the roll onto the stomach that the sentence describes.

**Tip:** Think of a plank held prone: the face is towards the floor.

Both terms keep their anatomical directions here, so the instruction is described correctly.

**E) "Apathy" is an absence of feeling or interest while "antipathy" is active dislike, so voters who cannot be bothered to turn out display "apathy" rather than antipathy.**

"Apathy" is the flat absence of engagement, the state of not caring enough to act, which is what non-voting most often reflects. "Antipathy" is a settled hostility directed at someone or something, and it usually takes towards or to, as in antipathy towards the whole political class. Staying at home out of indifference is the absence rather than the hostility.

The described behaviour is disengagement rather than aversion, so the distinction as drawn is exactly right.
tasks.solution_overview: Three of these items test whether a definition has been attached to the right member of a pair, so name both meanings for yourself before judging the claim: importance against mere pastness, believing against believable, imposed obligation against inner compulsion. The last two ask you to check a definition that is already correct, which is just as common in an exam as a reversal. Ask in every case whether the example given would still make sense with the other word in place.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements about near-homophones that survive into published prose. Judge each on standard meaning rather than on how alike the two words sound.
statements: "Elicit" is a verb meaning to draw a response out of someone, so an interviewer can "elicit" candid answers, whereas "illicit" is an adjective meaning unlawful.
"Defuse" means to make a dangerous situation less tense, so a mediator who calms a standoff between two villages has "defused" it, while "diffuse" means spread out or thinly scattered.
"Ingenuous" is the adjective for a clever invention, so a self-watering seed tray designed by a school pupil would be described as an "ingenuous" solution.
"Mitigate" means to count as evidence against something, so a court would say that repeated absences "mitigate" against granting bail.
A "hoard" is a store of hidden valuables and a "horde" is a large crowd, so archaeologists who unearth buried Roman coins have found a "hoard".
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Elicit" is a verb meaning to draw a response out of someone, so an interviewer can "elicit" candid answers, whereas "illicit" is an adjective meaning unlawful.**

"Elicit" is transitive and takes a response as its object: researchers elicit answers, symptoms or a reaction from a subject. "Illicit" is an adjective describing what the law or a rule forbids, as in illicit trade or an illicit substance. The sentence assigns each form to its own part of speech and to a context that fits it.

**Tip:** If the slot needs a doing word, only the e-spelling can fill it.

Verb and adjective are kept apart exactly as standard usage requires, so this account holds up.

**B) "Defuse" means to make a dangerous situation less tense, so a mediator who calms a standoff between two villages has "defused" it, while "diffuse" means spread out or thinly scattered.**

"Defuse" literally removes the fuse from a device and figuratively takes the danger out of a confrontation, which is what mediation between hostile parties aims at. "Diffuse" as a verb means to spread widely and as an adjective means scattered or wordy, as in diffuse light or a diffuse argument. Calming a standoff is the removal of danger, not a spreading out.

Defusing tension is exactly the metaphor the situation calls for, so the contrast drawn here is accurate.

**C) "Ingenuous" is the adjective for a clever invention, so a self-watering seed tray designed by a school pupil would be described as an "ingenuous" solution.**

"Ingenious" means inventive and cleverly contrived, and it attaches naturally to devices, designs and solutions. "Ingenuous" means innocent, open and unguarded, describing people rather than machinery, as in an ingenuous confession. A seed tray praised for its design is being called clever, not artless.

**Trap:** The negative "disingenuous", meaning insincere, is formed from the innocence word, not from the cleverness one.

Inventiveness is what the example celebrates, so the adjective offered is the wrong relative: it is an "ingenious" solution.

**D) "Mitigate" means to count as evidence against something, so a court would say that repeated absences "mitigate" against granting bail.**

"Militate against" means to be a strong factor working towards preventing something, and it is the verb that fits a court weighing reasons to refuse bail. "Mitigate" is transitive without a preposition and means to make something less severe, as in mitigating damage, a sentence or a risk. Nothing in this sentence is being softened; a consideration is telling against a decision.

**Trap:** "Mitigate against" is one of the most persistent slips in formal prose precisely because the two verbs sound alike.

The reasoning is about weight against a decision, so the verb here is the wrong one — repeated absences "militate" against granting bail.

**E) A "hoard" is a store of hidden valuables and a "horde" is a large crowd, so archaeologists who unearth buried Roman coins have found a "hoard".**

"Hoard" names a cache that someone has amassed and concealed, which is the standard term for buried coins or metalwork recovered from a field. "Horde" names a swarming multitude, originally a nomadic troop, and is used of people or animals rather than objects. Coins in the ground are a store of valuables, so the first noun belongs.

**Tip:** A hoard is hidden; a horde arrives.

The find is a cache rather than a crowd, so the pairing as stated is correct.
tasks.solution_overview: Word class settles two of these items before meaning does, since one member of the pair is a verb and the other an adjective or a noun. For the remaining lines, decide which direction the action runs and what the object of the verb has to be: you elicit answers, you defuse tension, and evidence militates against a conclusion. Reading each example aloud with the rival word substituted exposes the mismatch quickly.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Five short judgements about vocabulary in editorial, clinical and administrative writing. Decide whether each judgement reflects how the word is actually used.
statements: "Loath" is an adjective meaning reluctant and "loathe" is a verb meaning to detest, so a curator who is "loath" to move a fragile manuscript is unwilling rather than disgusted.
"Disinterested" is the precise word for a juror who finds the evidence boring, since it means lacking any interest in the proceedings.
"Emend" is the specialist verb for correcting a text, so an editor who removes a copyist's error from a medieval chronicle has "emended" it, while a legislature "amends" a bill.
"Apprise" means to inform someone and "appraise" means to assess value, so a finance director who tells the board about a supplier's price rise has "apprised" them, not appraised them.
"Systemic" describes something that affects an entire system, so a pathologist writing about an infection that has spread through the bloodstream calls it "systemic" rather than systematic.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Loath" is an adjective meaning reluctant and "loathe" is a verb meaning to detest, so a curator who is "loath" to move a fragile manuscript is unwilling rather than disgusted.**

"Loath" is predicative and normally followed by to plus a verb: loath to interfere, loath to commit. "Loathe" is a strong transitive verb of disgust and takes a direct object, as in loathing the smell of formalin. The curator's hesitation over a fragile item is reluctance, which is what the adjective conveys.

**Tip:** The final e brings the hatred; without it you have only unwillingness.

Reluctance rather than revulsion is what the example describes, so the distinction is drawn correctly.

**B) "Disinterested" is the precise word for a juror who finds the evidence boring, since it means lacking any interest in the proceedings.**

"Disinterested" means having no stake in the outcome, which is why we prize a disinterested arbiter, expert or observer. "Uninterested" means bored or unengaged, and that is the state the example actually describes. A juror who has stopped paying attention is uninterested, whereas a juror with no financial or personal stake is disinterested and therefore fit to serve.

**Trap:** In legal writing the two senses point in opposite directions: one disqualifies a juror, the other qualifies one.

Boredom belongs to the other adjective, so this definition misses — such a juror is "uninterested" in the evidence.

**C) "Emend" is the specialist verb for correcting a text, so an editor who removes a copyist's error from a medieval chronicle has "emended" it, while a legislature "amends" a bill.**

"Emend" belongs to textual scholarship and means to correct errors in a manuscript or edition, which is exactly what removing a scribal slip amounts to. "Amend" is the general verb for altering a document, law or plan, and it is the term parliaments use for changes to a bill. The chronicle is being corrected rather than revised in policy terms.

**Tip:** Editors emend; assemblies amend.

Each verb sits in its own professional home here, so the statement is accurate.

**D) "Apprise" means to inform someone and "appraise" means to assess value, so a finance director who tells the board about a supplier's price rise has "apprised" them, not appraised them.**

"Apprise" takes a person as its object and usually adds of: apprise the board of a development, apprise staff of a decision. "Appraise" takes a thing and means to evaluate its worth or quality, as in appraising a warehouse or an employee's performance. Passing news of a price rise to a board is informing people, not valuing an asset.

**Trap:** The board could be apprised of an appraisal, which is why the two verbs collide so often in reporting.

Telling is the action described, so the verb chosen in the example is the right one.

**E) "Systemic" describes something that affects an entire system, so a pathologist writing about an infection that has spread through the bloodstream calls it "systemic" rather than systematic.**

"Systemic" means pertaining to or affecting the whole of a body or structure, as in systemic circulation, systemic risk or systemic bias. "Systematic" means methodical, done according to a plan, as in a systematic search of the literature. An infection that has left the original site and reached the whole organism is a matter of extent, not method.

The pathologist is describing reach rather than procedure, so the word chosen fits the meaning intended.
tasks.solution_overview: Two of these pairs separate a verb from an adjective, and two separate a specialist verb from its everyday cousin, so identify the grammatical slot first and the shade of meaning second. Watch for the item that offers a plausible definition for the wrong member of the pair, which is the standard trick with disinterested. Where a technical field owns one word, as medicine owns systemic, let that ownership settle the choice.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Five accurate-looking claims about confusable pairs in formal British English. Weigh each against ordinary usage before deciding.
statements: "Waive" means to give up a claim or requirement, so a tribunal that decides not to enforce a filing deadline has "waived" it.
The idiom for restraint comes from horse riding, so a health board that curbs unnecessary prescribing is "reining in" the practice rather than reigning it in.
"Home in on" is the phrase for closing on a target, so a radiologist who narrows attention to a single shadow on a scan "homes in on" it, while "hone" means to sharpen.
"Founder" means to fail completely or sink, so a treaty that collapses at its final session has "foundered", whereas a delegate who struggles on clumsily "flounders".
"Veracious" means truthful and "voracious" means insatiably hungry, so a diarist praised for accuracy is "veracious" while a reader who devours books is "voracious".
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Waive" means to give up a claim or requirement, so a tribunal that decides not to enforce a filing deadline has "waived" it.**

"Waive" is a transitive verb of relinquishment: you waive a right, a fee, a rule or a period of notice. "Wave" belongs to the hand or the sea and cannot take an abstract entitlement as its object. A tribunal choosing not to insist on a deadline is surrendering a requirement it was entitled to enforce.

**Tip:** The related noun is "waiver", a document that gives something up.

Relinquishment is exactly what the sentence reports, so the usage described is correct.

**B) The idiom for restraint comes from horse riding, so a health board that curbs unnecessary prescribing is "reining in" the practice rather than reigning it in.**

"Rein" is the strap that controls a horse, which gives us rein in, free rein and keep a tight rein on something. "Reign" is what a monarch does and never governs an object in this idiom, so reigning in a practice makes no sense. Curbing prescribing is restraint applied to an activity, which is the riding metaphor.

**Trap:** "Free rein" is misspelled as "free reign" so often that the error now looks respectable.

The image behind the phrase is the bridle rather than the throne, so the correction offered here is well founded.

**C) "Home in on" is the phrase for closing on a target, so a radiologist who narrows attention to a single shadow on a scan "homes in on" it, while "hone" means to sharpen.**

"Home in on" comes from homing pigeons and guided missiles and describes movement towards a precise point. "Hone" means to sharpen a blade or refine a skill, so you hone an argument or hone your technique, but you cannot hone in on a shadow. Narrowing attention to one feature of an image is target-seeking, not sharpening.

**Tip:** If a target is named after the verb, the phrase is home in on.

The sentence describes converging on a point, so the phrasing recommended is the standard one.

**D) "Founder" means to fail completely or sink, so a treaty that collapses at its final session has "foundered", whereas a delegate who struggles on clumsily "flounders".**

"Founder" is what a ship does when it fills and goes down, and by extension what a plan, project or negotiation does when it fails outright. "Flounder" is to thrash about helplessly, like someone stuck in mud, and it implies continuing struggle rather than collapse. A treaty that dies at the last session has gone under rather than floundered on.

**Tip:** Foundering ends the story; floundering merely makes it painful.

Total failure is the outcome described, so the pairing in this statement is right.

**E) "Veracious" means truthful and "voracious" means insatiably hungry, so a diarist praised for accuracy is "veracious" while a reader who devours books is "voracious".**

"Veracious" shares its root with veracity and verify and describes a person or account that tells the truth. "Voracious" shares its root with devour and describes an appetite, whether for food or, figuratively, for reading and information. Praise for a diarist's accuracy concerns truthfulness, while a hunger for books concerns appetite.

Each adjective is matched to the quality it actually names, so the contrast stands as written.
tasks.solution_overview: Every line here rests on an idiom or a fixed metaphor, so recover the literal picture behind each word: a right given up, a horse restrained, a missile closing on a target, a ship going down. Once the image is clear, the choice between the two spellings usually settles itself. Notice too that several of these pairs are distinguished in speech only by context, which is why the surrounding words carry the weight.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Claims about pairs whose spellings differ by a letter or two but whose meanings do not overlap at all. Decide whether each account of meaning is correct.
statements: "Proscribe" means to forbid, so a statute that bans a pesticide "proscribes" it, while a doctor who recommends a treatment "prescribes" it.
"Censor" is the verb for formally condemning conduct, so a parliament that passes a motion criticising a minister has "censored" that minister.
"Prosecute" belongs to legal proceedings and "persecute" to sustained ill-treatment, so a state that hounds a religious minority "persecutes" it even when no charges are ever brought.
"Biennial" describes something that happens twice a year, so a conference held each June and December is a "biennial" event.
"Childlike" is the disapproving term, so a critic who dismisses a politician's sulking would call the behaviour "childlike".
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Proscribe" means to forbid, so a statute that bans a pesticide "proscribes" it, while a doctor who recommends a treatment "prescribes" it.**

"Proscribe" means to prohibit or outlaw, and it is the verb used of banned substances, banned organisations and outlawed practices. "Prescribe" means to lay down as a rule or to order a treatment, so regulations prescribe procedures and clinicians prescribe drugs. A statute banning a chemical is forbidding it, while a doctor issuing a course of treatment is ordering one.

**Tip:** Pro- here works like the pro- of prohibit, not like the pro- of promote.

The two verbs are matched to prohibition and instruction in the right order, so the account is accurate.

**B) "Censor" is the verb for formally condemning conduct, so a parliament that passes a motion criticising a minister has "censored" that minister.**

"Censure" is formal condemnation expressed by a body with standing to give it, which is why assemblies pass motions of censure. "Censor" means to suppress material judged unacceptable, so a wartime office censors letters and a board censors a film. A parliamentary motion attacks conduct rather than deleting text.

**Trap:** The nouns diverge too: a censure is a rebuke, a censor is an official with scissors.

Condemnation rather than suppression is what a motion delivers, so the sentence uses the wrong verb — the parliament has "censured" the minister.

**C) "Prosecute" belongs to legal proceedings and "persecute" to sustained ill-treatment, so a state that hounds a religious minority "persecutes" it even when no charges are ever brought.**

"Prosecute" means to bring criminal proceedings against someone, and it presupposes a court, a charge and a prosecutor. "Persecute" means to subject a person or group to persistent hostility because of who they are, and it needs no legal machinery whatsoever. Harassment of a minority without charges is oppression, not litigation.

**Tip:** A state can persecute thousands while prosecuting none, which is exactly the distinction the sentence draws.

The example turns on sustained mistreatment outside the courts, so the contrast is correctly stated.

**D) "Biennial" describes something that happens twice a year, so a conference held each June and December is a "biennial" event.**

"Biennial" means occurring every second year, which is also why a biennial plant takes two seasons to complete its life cycle. "Biannual" is the word for twice within a single year, though careful writers often replace it with "twice-yearly" precisely because readers mistrust it. Two meetings inside one calendar year fall under the twice-yearly sense.

**Trap:** Where ambiguity would matter, spell the interval out rather than relying on either bi- word.

The frequency described is twice a year, so the label attached is the wrong one: the conference is a "biannual" event.

**E) "Childlike" is the disapproving term, so a critic who dismisses a politician's sulking would call the behaviour "childlike".**

"Childish" is the pejorative member of the pair and marks behaviour as immature, petulant or unworthy of an adult. "Childlike" is warm or neutral and picks out the appealing qualities of childhood, such as childlike wonder, trust or delight. Dismissing a sulk is criticism, so the pejorative form is required.

**Tip:** The suffix -ish often sours a word, as in mannish or sheepish.

Disapproval is the whole point of the remark, so the term offered is the affectionate one instead: the critic would call it "childish".
tasks.solution_overview: Prefixes do most of the work in this set: pro- forbidding against pre- recommending, per- hounding against pro- taking to court, bi- twice a year against bi- every second year. Read the prefix, then check the example against it rather than trusting the family resemblance of the two words. The final item is a reminder that a shared root can still carry opposite attitudes, one approving and one dismissive.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Five statements about vocabulary used in research and reporting. Decide whether each one describes standard meaning and usage.
statements: "Obsolescent" means going out of use but not yet gone, so a hospital scanner still in service while its replacement is installed is "obsolescent" rather than obsolete.
"Enormity" is the neutral word for great size, so a geographer describing the sheer scale of an ice sheet should write about its "enormity".
"Fortuitous" strictly means happening by chance, so a chance alignment of two archive documents is "fortuitous" whether or not it turns out to be lucky.
"Ambivalent" describes a sentence that is open to more than one reading, so a clause that two courts have interpreted differently is "ambivalent".
"Endemic" means regularly found in a particular place or population, so malaria that persists year after year in a region is "endemic", while a sudden surge in cases is an epidemic.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Obsolescent" means going out of use but not yet gone, so a hospital scanner still in service while its replacement is installed is "obsolescent" rather than obsolete.**

"Obsolescent" describes a thing in the process of becoming outdated, still functioning but on the way out. "Obsolete" describes what has already fallen out of use entirely, like a discontinued format no machine can now read. A scanner still imaging patients during a handover period is at the earlier stage.

**Tip:** The -escent ending marks a process in progress, as in convalescent and luminescent.

The equipment is on its way out rather than out of use, so the distinction drawn here is exact.

**B) "Enormity" is the neutral word for great size, so a geographer describing the sheer scale of an ice sheet should write about its "enormity".**

"Enormity" traditionally means monstrous wickedness, as in the enormity of the crimes uncovered by a commission. Sheer size is carried by "enormousness", "immensity" or "vast scale", none of which import a moral verdict. An ice sheet is large rather than wicked, so a careful geographer avoids the moral noun.

**Trap:** The size sense is now common, but in edited academic prose it still reads as a slip.

Scale without moral judgement is what the description needs, so the recommendation misfires — the writer wants the "immensity" of the ice sheet.

**C) "Fortuitous" strictly means happening by chance, so a chance alignment of two archive documents is "fortuitous" whether or not it turns out to be lucky.**

"Fortuitous" derives from fortuit-, by chance, and describes accidental occurrence without any claim about benefit. "Fortunate" is the word that carries good luck, and it is what most people mean when they reach for the longer adjective. Two documents that happen to align were not planned to, which is chance pure and simple.

**Tip:** A fortuitous meeting can be a disaster; a fortunate one cannot.

The example insists on accident rather than good luck, so the definition given is faithful to the strict sense.

**D) "Ambivalent" describes a sentence that is open to more than one reading, so a clause that two courts have interpreted differently is "ambivalent".**

"Ambiguous" describes language that will bear more than one interpretation, which is exactly the complaint against a clause read two ways. "Ambivalent" describes a person holding conflicting feelings about something, as in ambivalent about the reform. Texts are ambiguous; minds are ambivalent.

**Trap:** Both begin with ambi-, both, but one doubles the meanings and the other doubles the attitudes.

The problem lies in the wording rather than in anyone's feelings, so the term is misapplied — such a clause is "ambiguous".

**E) "Endemic" means regularly found in a particular place or population, so malaria that persists year after year in a region is "endemic", while a sudden surge in cases is an epidemic.**

"Endemic" describes a disease that is constantly present at a baseline level in a defined area, which is how epidemiologists speak of malaria in parts of the tropics. "Epidemic" describes a sharp rise above that expected level, and "pandemic" extends such a rise across continents. Persistent year-round presence is the baseline sense.

**Tip:** Endemic answers where and always; epidemic answers how many and how fast.

Steady local presence is what the example specifies, so the definition matches the term.
tasks.solution_overview: Two of these items test a word whose careful sense is narrower than its popular one, so ask what the word meant before loose use widened it: chance rather than luck, moral outrage rather than mere size. Two more test a genuine technical contrast, obsolescent against obsolete and endemic against epidemic, where the difference is a matter of stage or of geography. The remaining line hides a swap between a property of a text and a property of a mind.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Judgements about words that appear in scientific, legal and journalistic commentary. Decide whether each judgement matches accepted usage.
statements: "Corroborate" means to confirm with further evidence, so a second ice core that supports the first team's dating "corroborates" it rather than collaborates with it.
"Incredulous" describes a claim too far-fetched to believe, so a report of a river running uphill would be called "incredulous".
"Judicious" means showing good judgement, so a curator's careful choice of three paintings for a small room is "judicious", while "judicial" belongs to courts and judges.
"Tortuous" means full of twists, so a mountain road that doubles back on itself is "tortuous", whereas "torturous" means causing suffering.
"Inflammable" means easily set alight, so a solvent stored in a laboratory cupboard is "inflammable", while "inflammatory" describes language that stirs anger.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Corroborate" means to confirm with further evidence, so a second ice core that supports the first team's dating "corroborates" it rather than collaborates with it.**

"Corroborate" takes evidence or a claim as its object and means to strengthen it with independent support. "Collaborate" means to work together and takes a person or institution after with, so teams collaborate but data cannot. A second core supporting the first is independent confirmation of a finding.

**Tip:** If the object is a fact rather than a colleague, the verb is corroborate.

Evidence supporting evidence is the relation described, so the sentence uses the right verb.

**B) "Incredulous" describes a claim too far-fetched to believe, so a report of a river running uphill would be called "incredulous".**

"Incredible" describes the claim that cannot be believed, and in careful prose it keeps that literal force rather than meaning merely excellent. "Incredulous" describes the hearer who refuses to believe, as in an incredulous audience or an incredulous stare. A report is a claim, not a listener.

**Trap:** Pair them by who is doing what: the story is incredible, the reader is incredulous.

The adjective has been moved from the audience to the account, so the label fails — such a report would be called "incredible".

**C) "Judicious" means showing good judgement, so a curator's careful choice of three paintings for a small room is "judicious", while "judicial" belongs to courts and judges.**

"Judicious" praises the quality of a decision and can describe anyone who chooses wisely, from an editor to a curator. "Judicial" is a relational adjective meaning of or by the courts, as in judicial review, judicial appointment or judicial reasoning. Selecting three works for a cramped gallery is a matter of good judgement, not of legal authority.

**Tip:** Judicial has no gradations; nothing is very judicial, but a choice can be highly judicious.

Wisdom rather than jurisdiction is at issue, so the description is correct.

**D) "Tortuous" means full of twists, so a mountain road that doubles back on itself is "tortuous", whereas "torturous" means causing suffering.**

"Tortuous" comes from torquere, to twist, and applies to winding roads, rivers and, figuratively, to convoluted arguments or negotiations. "Torturous" is built on torture and describes what inflicts pain, physical or mental. A road that doubles back is geometrically twisted, whatever the driver feels about it.

**Tip:** A tortuous explanation is merely complicated; a torturous one hurts.

Shape rather than suffering is what the example reports, so the pairing is sound.

**E) "Inflammable" means easily set alight, so a solvent stored in a laboratory cupboard is "inflammable", while "inflammatory" describes language that stirs anger.**

"Inflammable" means capable of catching fire, the in- being intensive rather than negative, which is why safety labels now prefer the unambiguous "flammable". "Inflammatory" describes speech or writing designed to provoke, and in medicine an inflammatory response in tissue. A solvent is a fire risk, not a rhetorical one.

**Trap:** Reading the in- as a negative here is a genuine safety hazard, not just a usage error.

Combustibility is the property the sentence names, so the account holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these lines are correct as they stand, which means the work lies in confirming a definition rather than hunting for a reversal. Check the object each verb or adjective takes: evidence corroborates a finding, a road twists, a chemical catches fire, a speech stirs anger. The one faulty line moves an adjective from a person to a claim, which is the classic route by which incredulous goes wrong.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Each line makes a confident claim about a word that is easy to misuse in formal writing. Decide whether the claim is correct.
statements: "Specious" simply means fake or forged, so a letter proved not to be by the author whose name it bears is best called a "specious" document.
"Connote" is the word for a term's literal reference, so saying that "canine" "connotes" a dog states its dictionary meaning.
"Practicable" describes a person who is good with their hands, so an engineer who repairs the pump herself is "practicable".
"Prophecy" is the verb and "prophesy" the noun, so a chronicler "prophecies" a famine and records the "prophesy" in the margin.
"Arbitration" is the settlement of a dispute by an appointed third party, so a supplier and a retailer who take a contract quarrel to a private tribunal are in "arbitration", not arbitrage.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Specious" simply means fake or forged, so a letter proved not to be by the author whose name it bears is best called a "specious" document.**

"Spurious" means false, counterfeit or of illegitimate origin, which is precisely what a misattributed letter is. "Specious" means superficially convincing yet wrong, and it attaches to arguments and reasoning rather than to objects. A forged document is fake in origin, not merely persuasive on the surface.

**Tip:** A specious argument seduces; a spurious relic deceives.

Origin rather than plausibility is the issue with a misattributed letter, so the term chosen misses — the document is "spurious".

**B) "Connote" is the word for a term's literal reference, so saying that "canine" "connotes" a dog states its dictionary meaning.**

"Denote" names what a word literally refers to, its dictionary reference: canine denotes a dog. "Connote" names the associations a word carries beyond that reference, so "canine" may connote loyalty, watchfulness or menace depending on context. The example is about the plain reference, not the halo of associations.

**Tip:** Denotation is in the dictionary; connotation is in the culture.

Literal reference is what the sentence describes, so the verb attached to it is wrong — "canine" "denotes" a dog.

**C) "Practicable" describes a person who is good with their hands, so an engineer who repairs the pump herself is "practicable".**

"Practicable" means capable of being carried out, and it describes plans, routes and repairs rather than people: a practicable solution, as soon as practicable. "Practical" is the adjective for a person with hands-on ability, and also for what is useful rather than theoretical. An engineer who fixes the pump herself is practical; the fix itself may be practicable.

**Trap:** Only one of the two words can describe a human being, and it is the shorter one.

The sentence is describing a person, so the adjective offered cannot apply — that engineer is "practical".

**D) "Prophecy" is the verb and "prophesy" the noun, so a chronicler "prophecies" a famine and records the "prophesy" in the margin.**

"Prophecy", ending in -cy and rhyming with see, is the noun for the prediction itself. "Prophesy", ending in -sy and rhyming with sigh, is the verb for making it. The chronicler performs the act and then writes down the thing, so the forms in this sentence have been exchanged.

**Tip:** The verb has the s of "say"; the noun has the c of "claim".

Both labels sit on the wrong form here, so the sentence fails — the chronicler "prophesies" a famine and records the "prophecy".

**E) "Arbitration" is the settlement of a dispute by an appointed third party, so a supplier and a retailer who take a contract quarrel to a private tribunal are in "arbitration", not arbitrage.**

"Arbitration" is a form of dispute resolution in which the parties accept the decision of an appointed arbitrator instead of going to court. "Arbitrage" is the trading practice of profiting from price differences for the same asset in different markets. A contract quarrel heard by a private tribunal is dispute resolution.

**Tip:** Arbitration ends an argument; arbitrage exploits a gap.

The scenario describes a hearing rather than a trade, so the term used is the right one.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these definitions have been attached to the wrong member of a pair, so build each contrast for yourself before reading the example: plausible but wrong against outright false, literal reference against emotional association, capable of being done against sensible in practice. One item also tests which spelling is the verb, a distinction that survives only in careful prose. Treat any definition that sounds neatly symmetrical as the one most likely to have been reversed.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Five statements about medical, scientific and social vocabulary. Decide whether each describes its word correctly.
statements: "Diagnosis" identifies what a condition is and "prognosis" forecasts how it will develop, so a consultant who predicts recovery within a year is offering a "prognosis".
A "stimulus" is anything that provokes a response, while a "stimulant" is a substance that raises physiological activity, so a flash of light used in an experiment is a "stimulus".
"Regimen" is a prescribed course of treatment or exercise and "regime" is a system of government, so a physiotherapist sets out a daily "regimen" of stretches.
"Sensuous" appeals to the senses generally and "sensual" carries an erotic charge, so a critic praising the rich texture of a landscape painting calls it "sensuous".
"Urban" relates to towns and cities while "urbane" describes polished, courteous manners, so a diplomat known for smooth conversation is "urbane".
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Diagnosis" identifies what a condition is and "prognosis" forecasts how it will develop, so a consultant who predicts recovery within a year is offering a "prognosis".**

"Diagnosis" answers the question of identification: which disease or disorder accounts for the findings. "Prognosis" answers the question of outlook: how the condition is expected to progress, with or without treatment. A prediction of recovery within a year is a statement about the future course of the illness.

**Tip:** The prefixes do the work: dia- through the signs, pro- ahead in time.

Naming and forecasting are kept in their proper roles, so the statement is accurate.

**B) A "stimulus" is anything that provokes a response, while a "stimulant" is a substance that raises physiological activity, so a flash of light used in an experiment is a "stimulus".**

"Stimulus" is the general term in psychology and physiology for whatever triggers a reaction, from a sound to a change in temperature. "Stimulant" is narrower and names a substance such as caffeine that increases activity in the nervous system. A flash of light in a laboratory trial is a trigger rather than a drug.

**Tip:** The plural stimuli belongs to the trigger word, which is why lab reports are full of it.

Trigger and substance are correctly separated here, so the description holds.

**C) "Regimen" is a prescribed course of treatment or exercise and "regime" is a system of government, so a physiotherapist sets out a daily "regimen" of stretches.**

"Regimen" comes from the same root as regulate and names an ordered plan for health: a drug regimen, a training regimen, a dietary regimen. "Regime" names a governing order, usually with a critical edge, as in a military regime, though it also appears in technical phrases such as a flow regime. A physiotherapist's daily plan belongs to health rather than to politics.

**Tip:** The extra n keeps the word in the clinic.

The example is a treatment plan, so the term chosen fits it precisely.

**D) "Sensuous" appeals to the senses generally and "sensual" carries an erotic charge, so a critic praising the rich texture of a landscape painting calls it "sensuous".**

"Sensuous" was popularised to describe aesthetic pleasure taken through the senses without any sexual implication, which suits painting, music and prose style. "Sensual" points to bodily and especially erotic gratification, which is why it would misdescribe a landscape. Rich texture and colour appeal to the eye, so the aesthetic word is required.

**Tip:** Reviewers reach for sensuous exactly when they wish to avoid the other word's suggestion.

The praise concerns aesthetic effect rather than appetite, so the choice is well made.

**E) "Urban" relates to towns and cities while "urbane" describes polished, courteous manners, so a diplomat known for smooth conversation is "urbane".**

"Urban" is a classifying adjective: urban planning, urban populations, urban heat islands. "Urbane" is an evaluative one describing sophistication and easy politeness, a sense that grew from the idea of city manners. A diplomat praised for conversational polish is being credited with sophistication, not located in a city.

**Tip:** Only one of the pair can be used to compliment a person.

Manner rather than geography is what the sentence describes, so the distinction is drawn correctly.
tasks.solution_overview: This set rewards attention to what each noun or adjective is a word about: a name for an illness against a forecast of its course, the thing that provokes against the drug that stimulates, a system of government against a course of treatment. Two items also test connotation, where the difference between the members of a pair is one of tone rather than reference. If a definition sounds right, confirm it against the example rather than against the word's sound.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Five claims about pairs that share a root, a sound or a spelling. Decide whether each one gets the meaning and the word class right.
statements: "Contagious" and "infectious" are interchangeable in medicine, since both describe any disease caused by a pathogen regardless of how it spreads.
"Criterion" is singular and "criteria" plural, so a panel that applies a single test of eligibility is applying one "criterion".
"Verbal" is the precise term for something spoken rather than written, so careful legal prose describes an agreement made in conversation as a "verbal" agreement.
"Instil" means to introduce an attitude gradually, so a teacher who builds a habit of checking sources over a year has "instilled" it, while "install" means to put equipment or a person in place.
A question no longer worth arguing is a "mute" point, since "mute" means deprived of practical significance.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Contagious" and "infectious" are interchangeable in medicine, since both describe any disease caused by a pathogen regardless of how it spreads.**

"Contagious" describes an illness passed on by direct or indirect contact between hosts, which is why measles and scabies are contagious. "Infectious" is the wider term for any disease caused by a pathogen, including those carried by mosquitoes or contaminated water and never passed hand to hand. Tetanus is infectious but not contagious, so the two labels cannot be swapped.

**Trap:** Everyday speech treats them as synonyms, but epidemiology keeps the transmission route in view.

Route of transmission separates the terms, so the claim of interchangeability does not survive contact with the medical sense.

**B) "Criterion" is singular and "criteria" plural, so a panel that applies a single test of eligibility is applying one "criterion".**

"Criterion" keeps its Greek singular, and "criteria" is the plural, exactly as phenomenon pairs with phenomena. A panel weighing one standard is therefore applying a criterion, and only a list of standards would be criteria. Treating the plural as a singular, as in "the main criteria is", is the usual slip.

**Tip:** If you can say "this one", the form you need ends in -on.

The example involves a single standard, so the number described is right.

**C) "Verbal" is the precise term for something spoken rather than written, so careful legal prose describes an agreement made in conversation as a "verbal" agreement.**

"Oral" means by mouth and is the precise term for what is spoken, which is why lawyers write of oral evidence, oral submissions and an oral contract. "Verbal" strictly means expressed in words, so a written contract is verbal too, and that ambiguity is why careful drafters avoid it. An agreement reached in conversation is spoken rather than merely worded.

**Trap:** In everyday speech verbal has taken over, but in drafting the ambiguity can be costly.

Precision in legal prose favours the mouth word, so the claim does not hold — such an agreement is an "oral" agreement.

**D) "Instil" means to introduce an attitude gradually, so a teacher who builds a habit of checking sources over a year has "instilled" it, while "install" means to put equipment or a person in place.**

"Instil" comes from the idea of adding drop by drop and takes abstract objects: instil confidence, discipline or a habit, usually in someone. "Install" is physical or official and takes equipment, software or an office-holder, as in installing a boiler or installing a new dean. A habit formed over a school year is built up gradually rather than fitted.

**Tip:** If the object cannot be unplugged, the verb is instil.

Gradual formation of a habit is exactly what the first verb names, so the contrast is accurate.

**E) A question no longer worth arguing is a "mute" point, since "mute" means deprived of practical significance.**

"Moot" is the adjective for a question that is arguable in theory but of no practical consequence, a sense that comes from the moot courts where students debated hypothetical cases. "Mute" means silent or unable to speak and belongs to voices, not to arguments. A question that no longer matters is moot regardless of how loudly anyone discusses it.

**Trap:** The error survives because the two are near-homophones in rapid speech.

Practical irrelevance is the sense required, so the spelling given is wrong — the question is a "moot" point.
tasks.solution_overview: Two lines here quietly collapse a real distinction, treating two words as interchangeable when the technical or legal sense keeps them apart. Two others test number and form, where a singular has been mistaken for a plural or a verb of gradual instilling for one of physical fitting. Look for the word that a specialist field defines narrowly, and let that narrow definition decide the claim.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Statements about verbs and adjectives that appear in reporting on courts, conservation and public life. Decide whether each is correct.
statements: "Phase" is the verb meaning to disconcert, so a witness unshaken by hostile cross-examination is described as not being "phased" by it.
"Libel" is defamation in permanent form and "slander" is spoken, so a false accusation printed in a newspaper is "libel".
"Wreak" means to cause or inflict, so a storm surge that tears through a coastal marsh has "wreaked" havoc on it.
"Forgo" means to do without, so a researcher who gives up a sabbatical to finish an excavation "forgoes" it, while "forego" means to go before.
"Hypercritical" is the word for someone who condemns in others what they do themselves, so a campaigner who flies weekly while denouncing air travel is being "hypercritical".
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Phase" is the verb meaning to disconcert, so a witness unshaken by hostile cross-examination is described as not being "phased" by it.**

"Faze" means to disconcert or unsettle and appears almost always in the negative: nothing fazes her, he was not fazed. "Phase" as a verb means to carry out in stages, as in phasing in a regulation or phasing out a chemical. A witness who remains composed is undisturbed rather than introduced by instalments.

**Tip:** If you can substitute "rattled", the spelling is faze.

Composure under pressure is the point, so the spelling offered is the wrong one — the witness was not "fazed" by the questioning.

**B) "Libel" is defamation in permanent form and "slander" is spoken, so a false accusation printed in a newspaper is "libel".**

"Libel" covers defamatory material fixed in a lasting medium, which historically meant print and now includes broadcast and online publication. "Slander" covers transient spoken defamation and traditionally required proof of actual loss. A false accusation set in type is fixed and published, which puts it squarely in the first category.

**Tip:** Permanence, not severity, decides which term applies.

The medium described is print, so the classification given is correct.

**C) "Wreak" means to cause or inflict, so a storm surge that tears through a coastal marsh has "wreaked" havoc on it.**

"Wreak" is a transitive verb of infliction and survives mainly in wreak havoc, wreak vengeance and wreak destruction, with the past tense wreaked. "Wreck" means to destroy or ruin a thing outright and takes the object destroyed, as in wrecking a ship. Havoc is what gets wreaked, not what gets wrecked.

**Trap:** The old past form "wrought" belongs to work, not to wreak, though it is often borrowed here.

The idiom and its object match, so the sentence uses the verb correctly.

**D) "Forgo" means to do without, so a researcher who gives up a sabbatical to finish an excavation "forgoes" it, while "forego" means to go before.**

"Forgo" means to relinquish or abstain from something one could have had: forgo a fee, forgo an opportunity, forgo the right to appeal. "Forego" with the e means to precede, and it survives chiefly in the participle "foregoing", meaning already mentioned. Giving up a sabbatical is abstention rather than precedence.

**Tip:** Keep the e only when something goes before.

Relinquishment is what the researcher does, so the definition offered is accurate.

**E) "Hypercritical" is the word for someone who condemns in others what they do themselves, so a campaigner who flies weekly while denouncing air travel is being "hypercritical".**

"Hypocritical" describes the gap between a person's stated principles and their conduct, which is exactly the campaigner's position. "Hypercritical" means excessively fault-finding, from hyper- meaning over, and says nothing about the critic's own behaviour. Weekly flights alongside public denunciation of flying expose inconsistency rather than severity.

**Trap:** The two differ by one letter but by a whole moral charge.

Inconsistency between word and deed is the accusation, so the adjective supplied is the wrong one — the campaigner is being "hypocritical".
tasks.solution_overview: Three of these items are correct definitions of verbs that survive almost entirely in fixed phrases, so recover the phrase itself: wreak havoc, forgo a right, be fazed by pressure. The two false lines misassign a word class or a moral charge, which is how phase and hypercritical slip past a careless reader. Where a pair differs by a prefix, ask what that prefix contributes before accepting the definition offered.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Five judgements about words used in engineering, historical research and field science. Decide whether each judgement is accurate.
statements: "Obviate" means to remove a need or difficulty, so a drainage design that makes a pumping station unnecessary "obviates" it, while "obfuscate" means to make something deliberately unclear.
"Adduce" means to put evidence forward and "deduce" means to reach a conclusion from it, so a historian "adduces" three letters and then "deduces" the date of the meeting.
"Interpolate" is estimating a value between known data points and "extrapolate" is projecting beyond them, so a climatologist filling a gap between two measured years "interpolates".
"Deprecate" is the accounting verb for the decline in an asset's book value, so a haulage company's lorries "deprecate" over five years.
"Irruption" is a sudden invasion or influx, so ecologists describing a surge of crossbills into new woodland call it an "irruption", while an "eruption" bursts outward.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Obviate" means to remove a need or difficulty, so a drainage design that makes a pumping station unnecessary "obviates" it, while "obfuscate" means to make something deliberately unclear.**

"Obviate" means to head off a problem or dispense with a requirement, so a design can obviate the need for further work. "Obfuscate" means to muddy or darken, usually said of language that hides rather than reveals. A drainage scheme that removes the need for pumping has eliminated a requirement, not clouded one.

**Tip:** Obviate often appears with "the need for", which is a useful signal that the requirement disappears.

Elimination rather than concealment is what the design achieves, so the definitions are correctly assigned.

**B) "Adduce" means to put evidence forward and "deduce" means to reach a conclusion from it, so a historian "adduces" three letters and then "deduces" the date of the meeting.**

"Adduce" is what you do with evidence: you bring it forward in support of a case, which is why the verb takes documents, examples and citations as objects. "Deduce" is what you do with reasoning: you derive a conclusion from premises already on the table. Producing the letters comes first, and dating the meeting follows from them.

**Tip:** Ad- brings towards; de- takes away from.

The two steps are placed in their natural order here, so the account is accurate.

**C) "Interpolate" is estimating a value between known data points and "extrapolate" is projecting beyond them, so a climatologist filling a gap between two measured years "interpolates".**

"Interpolate" works inside the range of observation, inserting an estimate where a measurement is missing. "Extrapolate" reaches outside that range, projecting a trend forward or backward beyond the data, which is why it carries far more risk. A missing year that sits between two measured ones lies inside the range.

**Tip:** Inter- goes between; extra- goes beyond.

The gap being filled lies within the observed span, so the term chosen is the correct one.

**D) "Deprecate" is the accounting verb for the decline in an asset's book value, so a haulage company's lorries "deprecate" over five years.**

"Depreciate" is the verb for a fall in value, whether of a currency or of equipment written down over its useful life. "Deprecate" means to express disapproval of something, and in technical documentation it marks a feature as discouraged and due for removal. Lorries losing value on a balance sheet are being written down, not criticised.

**Trap:** "Self-deprecating" belongs to the disapproval word, which is why the pair keeps colliding.

Loss of value is what the example describes, so the verb attached to it is wrong — the lorries "depreciate" over five years.

**E) "Irruption" is a sudden invasion or influx, so ecologists describing a surge of crossbills into new woodland call it an "irruption", while an "eruption" bursts outward.**

"Irruption" is movement inward: a sudden entry of animals, people or forces into an area, and it is the standard term for periodic influxes of birds outside their usual range. "Eruption" is movement outward, whether of lava, steam or a rash. Birds arriving in unfamiliar woodland are coming in rather than bursting out.

**Tip:** The prefixes ir- and e- mark direction, in and out.

Direction of movement decides the term, so the ecologists' usage is described correctly.
tasks.solution_overview: Most of these pairs separate two stages of an intellectual operation: putting evidence forward against drawing a conclusion, filling a gap inside a dataset against projecting past its edge, removing a need against clouding an issue. Fix the direction of each operation and the false line becomes visible. One item also tests a pair whose spellings differ by a single letter while their fields, accounting and criticism, do not overlap at all.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Each statement below tests a rule-based contrast between two similar words from law, public administration and civic life. Decide whether the rule is stated correctly.
statements: "Venal" means open to bribery and "venial" means pardonable, so an inspector who takes payments to overlook faults is "venal" while a clerk's small filing error is "venial".
"Emoluments" are the payments and benefits attached to an office, so a company's annual report lists directors' "emoluments", whereas an "emollient" softens skin or tempers.
"Malfeasance" is wrongdoing that is unlawful in itself and "misfeasance" is a lawful act performed improperly, so a council officer who takes a bribe commits "malfeasance".
"Immunity" is a formal exemption from liability and "impunity" is escaping punishment in practice, so a witness granted a legal exemption from prosecution has "immunity".
"Sedition" is incitement against the authority of the state and "secession" is the withdrawal of a territory from it, so pamphlets urging soldiers to mutiny were charged as "sedition".
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Venal" means open to bribery and "venial" means pardonable, so an inspector who takes payments to overlook faults is "venal" while a clerk's small filing error is "venial".**

"Venal" describes a person or office that can be bought, and it extends to venal practices and a venal administration. "Venial" comes from the theology of forgivable sin and describes a minor, excusable fault, as opposed to a grave one. Taking payments to falsify inspections is corruption, while a misfiled form is a trivial slip.

**Tip:** The extra i marks the lighter offence.

Severity and corruptibility are correctly separated, so the rule as stated is right.

**B) "Emoluments" are the payments and benefits attached to an office, so a company's annual report lists directors' "emoluments", whereas an "emollient" softens skin or tempers.**

"Emolument" is the formal term for the salary, fees and benefits that flow from holding a post, which is why it appears in constitutions and remuneration reports. "Emollient" is a soothing substance in pharmacy and, figuratively, a soothing manner or statement, as in an emollient reply to critics. Sums disclosed for directors are payments for office.

**Tip:** One word pays; the other soothes.

The financial sense fits the annual report exactly, so the contrast is accurate.

**C) "Malfeasance" is wrongdoing that is unlawful in itself and "misfeasance" is a lawful act performed improperly, so a council officer who takes a bribe commits "malfeasance".**

"Malfeasance" names conduct that is illegal from the outset, such as accepting a bribe in public office. "Misfeasance" names the improper performance of an act that was lawful to begin with, such as issuing a licence carelessly, and "nonfeasance" is the failure to act at all. Bribery falls in the first class because no version of it is lawful.

**Tip:** Mal- bad in itself, mis- badly done, non- not done.

The example is unlawful in its own right, so the classification given holds.

**D) "Immunity" is a formal exemption from liability and "impunity" is escaping punishment in practice, so a witness granted a legal exemption from prosecution has "immunity".**

"Immunity" is conferred: a state grants diplomatic immunity, a prosecutor grants immunity from prosecution, and the exemption has a legal basis. "Impunity" describes the factual absence of consequences, which is why the usual phrase is "with impunity" for those who offend and go unpunished. A formal grant to a witness is the conferred exemption.

**Tip:** Immunity is on paper; impunity is in practice.

The grant described has legal standing, so the term applied to it is correct.

**E) "Sedition" is incitement against the authority of the state and "secession" is the withdrawal of a territory from it, so pamphlets urging soldiers to mutiny were charged as "sedition".**

"Sedition" covers speech or conduct that stirs rebellion against lawful authority without necessarily amounting to treason. "Secession" is the formal departure of a region or member from a union, an act of separation rather than incitement. Pamphlets aimed at provoking mutiny among troops are incitement.

**Tip:** Sedition stirs; secession leaves.

The charge described concerns incitement, so the definitions are correctly matched.
tasks.solution_overview: This set is built from pairs that share a root but split along a line of severity, formality or scope: corruptibility against pardonable fault, unlawful acts against lawful acts done badly, formal exemption against escape in practice. Say what each word covers and what it excludes before testing it against the example. Every line here defines both members, so a single misplaced boundary is what you are looking for.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Five definitions offered for words that often appear in policy and science journalism. Decide whether each definition belongs to the word it is attached to.
statements: "Perspicuous" describes a person with sharp insight, so a detective who reads a suspect's hesitation correctly is "perspicuous".
"Temerity" means shyness in the face of authority, so a student too nervous to question the professor showed "temerity".
"Meretricious" means showily attractive but hollow, so a reviewer who calls a novel's style "meretricious" is condemning it rather than praising it as meritorious.
"Noisome" is a formal word for loud, so a generator that keeps a whole village awake is "noisome".
"Fulsome" simply means generous and abundant, so a tribute described as "fulsome praise" is straightforwardly complimentary in careful usage.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Perspicuous" describes a person with sharp insight, so a detective who reads a suspect's hesitation correctly is "perspicuous".**

"Perspicacious" describes acute mental penetration in a person: a perspicacious reader, a perspicacious judge of character. "Perspicuous" describes clarity in expression, so an argument, a definition or a set of instructions can be perspicuous. A detective's insight is a quality of mind rather than of prose.

**Tip:** Perspicuity belongs to writing; perspicacity belongs to the writer.

Insight is what the example praises, so the adjective offered is the wrong member — that detective is "perspicacious".

**B) "Temerity" means shyness in the face of authority, so a student too nervous to question the professor showed "temerity".**

"Temerity" means reckless boldness or nerve, which is why it turns up in phrases like had the temerity to interrupt. "Timidity" is the fear-based quality the sentence actually describes, and the two are near-opposites despite their similar shape. A student who says nothing out of nerves is displaying the second, not the first.

**Trap:** Temerity is closer to audacity than to timidity, whatever the sound suggests.

The behaviour described is nervous silence, so the noun attached to it is inverted — the student showed "timidity".

**C) "Meretricious" means showily attractive but hollow, so a reviewer who calls a novel's style "meretricious" is condemning it rather than praising it as meritorious.**

"Meretricious" comes from a Latin word for hired flattery and describes surface glitter without substance, as in meretricious ornament or meretricious argument. "Meritorious" means deserving of praise and is straightforwardly positive. A reviewer using the first word is calling the style tawdry, however much it resembles the second.

**Trap:** The shared mer- makes the insult look like a compliment, which is precisely why it is misread.

The word carries its built-in contempt into the review, so the description of the reviewer's verdict is right.

**D) "Noisome" is a formal word for loud, so a generator that keeps a whole village awake is "noisome".**

"Noisome" has nothing to do with noise: it comes from the same root as annoy and means offensive, especially foul-smelling, as in noisome fumes from a landfill. Loudness is carried by clamorous, deafening or simply noisy. A generator that keeps a village awake is an assault on the ears rather than the nose.

**Trap:** The first syllable is a false friend, and it catches confident readers most often.

Sound rather than smell is at issue, so the definition supplied is mistaken — that generator is simply "noisy".

**E) "Fulsome" simply means generous and abundant, so a tribute described as "fulsome praise" is straightforwardly complimentary in careful usage.**

"Fulsome" in careful usage means excessive to the point of insincerity, so fulsome praise is praise that embarrasses rather than honours. The generous sense has revived in speech, but in edited prose the pejorative reading remains live and can invert a writer's intention. A tribute meant warmly is better called generous or wholehearted.

**Trap:** Because both senses are current, the word now says more about the reader than the subject.

The definition ignores the sense that still dominates in formal writing, so the claim cannot stand — "fulsome praise" reads as praise laid on too thick.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these lines hand a definition to the wrong twin, and the pattern is worth noticing: the harder, rarer word is given the easy everyday meaning. Ask what the rarer member actually contributes, whether that is clear expression, reckless boldness, a bad smell or excessive praise. The one true line resists that pull by keeping a showy word firmly negative.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Five statements about words used in laboratory, statistical and epidemiological writing. Decide whether each one reflects standard technical usage.
statements: "Homogeneous" means uniform in composition, so a metallurgist describing an alloy of even structure calls it "homogeneous", while "homogenous" belongs to biology and shared descent.
The "median" of a set of measurements is the arithmetic average, so adding all the values and dividing by their number gives the "median" river depth.
"Incidence" counts new cases arising in a period and "prevalence" counts all existing cases at a moment, so an epidemiologist tracking fresh diagnoses each month is measuring "incidence".
"Viscous" describes a thick, slow-flowing liquid, so lava that creeps rather than runs is "viscous", while "vicious" means savage or spiteful.
"Desiccate" means to scatter and gradually disappear, so heat spreading away from a cooling engine "desiccates".
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Homogeneous" means uniform in composition, so a metallurgist describing an alloy of even structure calls it "homogeneous", while "homogenous" belongs to biology and shared descent.**

"Homogeneous", with the -e- before -ous, means the same throughout, and it is the word for a well-mixed sample or a uniform population. "Homogenous" is a biological term for similarity arising from common ancestry, closer in meaning to homologous. An alloy of even composition is uniform rather than related by descent.

**Tip:** The longer spelling belongs to the everyday technical sense, which is the opposite of what most people guess.

Uniformity of composition is what the metallurgist means, so the account is correct.

**B) The "median" of a set of measurements is the arithmetic average, so adding all the values and dividing by their number gives the "median" river depth.**

The "mean" is the arithmetic average obtained by summing values and dividing by their count. The "median" is the middle value once the measurements are ranked, which is why it resists distortion by a few extreme readings. Summing and dividing is the definition of the first, not the second.

**Tip:** A single very deep channel pulls the mean down the page but barely moves the median.

The calculation described produces the average, so the label is misapplied — that figure is the "mean" river depth.

**C) "Incidence" counts new cases arising in a period and "prevalence" counts all existing cases at a moment, so an epidemiologist tracking fresh diagnoses each month is measuring "incidence".**

"Incidence" is a rate of onset: how many new cases appear in a defined population over a defined time. "Prevalence" is a snapshot: how many people have the condition at a given point, including those diagnosed years earlier. Counting fresh diagnoses month by month is a measure of onset.

**Tip:** A long-lasting illness can have low incidence and high prevalence at the same time.

New cases over time are what the example counts, so the term used is the right one.

**D) "Viscous" describes a thick, slow-flowing liquid, so lava that creeps rather than runs is "viscous", while "vicious" means savage or spiteful.**

"Viscous" is a physical property term: high viscosity means strong internal resistance to flow, as in tar, honey or silica-rich lava. "Vicious" describes cruelty or ferocity and belongs to behaviour, not to fluids. Lava that advances slowly is resisting flow.

**Tip:** The noun viscosity keeps the physical word anchored to measurement.

Flow behaviour is what the example describes, so the adjective fits.

**E) "Desiccate" means to scatter and gradually disappear, so heat spreading away from a cooling engine "desiccates".**

"Desiccate" means to dry out thoroughly, which is why we speak of desiccated coconut and of soils desiccated by drought. "Dissipate" means to disperse and fade away, and it is the standard verb for energy, heat or a crowd. Heat leaving an engine is being dispersed rather than dried.

**Tip:** Desiccation removes water; dissipation removes concentration.

The process described is dispersal of energy, so the verb chosen is wrong — the heat "dissipates".
tasks.solution_overview: Technical fields define several of these words far more tightly than everyday speech does, so let the discipline decide: statistics owns the difference between mean and median, epidemiology owns incidence against prevalence, and materials science owns viscosity. Two items also test a pair of near-twins whose difference is one letter but whose subjects are matter and biology. When a definition is offered, check it against how the specialists actually count or measure.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Statements about precise word choice in scientific, environmental and museum writing. Decide whether each is correct.
statements: "Salutary" means producing a beneficial, often corrective effect, so a near-miss that forces a laboratory to rewrite its safety protocol is a "salutary" lesson.
"Restive" means calm and rested, so a crowd waiting quietly outside the courtroom is "restive".
"Equable" is the adjective for a fair division, so a settlement that splits water rights justly between two provinces is "equable".
"Seasonable" means occurring at regular times of year, so bird migration that happens every autumn is "seasonable" movement.
"Provenance" is the record of where an object has come from, so a museum tracing a vase through three earlier collections is establishing its "provenance", not its providence.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Salutary" means producing a beneficial, often corrective effect, so a near-miss that forces a laboratory to rewrite its safety protocol is a "salutary" lesson.**

"Salutary" shares a root with salus, health, and describes something unpleasant that nevertheless does good, which is why the standard collocations are a salutary lesson, warning or reminder. "Salutatory" is the rare adjective meaning of or relating to a greeting. An accident that improves practice is corrective and beneficial.

**Tip:** The salutary experience is rarely enjoyable; that tension is built into the word.

Correction with benefit is exactly what the example reports, so the usage is right.

**B) "Restive" means calm and rested, so a crowd waiting quietly outside the courtroom is "restive".**

"Restive" means restless and hard to control, originally said of a horse that refuses to move as directed and now of impatient crowds and troops. "Restful" is the word for what produces calm, and "rested" for a person who has recovered. A quiet, patient crowd is the opposite of what the first adjective describes.

**Trap:** The rest- opening promises repose and delivers agitation.

The scene described is one of calm, so the adjective does not fit — such a crowd is anything but "restive".

**C) "Equable" is the adjective for a fair division, so a settlement that splits water rights justly between two provinces is "equable".**
